title: Oil Companies Are Begging the Supreme Court to Let Them Off the Hook For Climate Change - Balls and Strikes
content: Want more Balls & Strikes? Sign up for our free newsletter here. This article was published in partnership with Slate. The Supreme Court officially began its new term on Monday morning with oral argument in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County. Befitting an institution with vast power over the public despite historically low public support, the court’s opening case this term is about elite impunity: Suncor will determine whether communities may sue oil and gas companies in state court and hold them financially responsible for literally fueling climate change. Back in 2018, Boulder County filed a lawsuit in a Colorado state court against fossil fuel industry giants Suncor Energy and Exxon, alleging that the companies caused extensive—and expensive—alterations to Boulder’s climate. Boulder alleged that the companies knew that their unchecked production and promotion of fossil fuels would “result in dangerous changes in the climate,” but continued such activities anyway, and engaged in a decades-long campaign of “concealing” those dangers and “misrepresenting” them to the public. As a result, the complaint says, instead of snow in the winter, Boulder gets more “high-intensity, short-duration rainfall events” that overwhelm its drainage systems and cause flooding. Instead of rain in the spring, Boulder gets more droughts that “have substantial implications for agriculture, wildfires and water availability.” And instead of warm days in the summer, Boulder gets more heat waves that lead to “premature deaths” and “adverse economic impacts,” particularly on outdoor labor sectors like agriculture and construction. Boulder has already spent over $100 million repairing damage related to climate change, and expects to spend over $100 million more in order to adapt its infrastructure over the next 25 years, as it attempts to mitigate the effects of flooding, droughts, wildfires, and other harms. “Taxpayers cannot pay the full costs,” says the state’s complaint, “nor should they.” Climate change has a hefty price tag, which is why dozens of state and local governments like Boulder’s have filed lawsuits to force the culprits to help pay the costs. It’s also why polluters like Suncor Energy and Exxon are desperate to get the lawsuits thrown out of court. In 2022, however, a Colorado trial court denied Suncor’s motion to dismiss. And last year, the Colorado Supreme Court affirmed that decision, meaning Boulder’s lawsuit could finally move forward. So, the corporations turned to the U.S. Supreme Court for help. Specifically, the companies are asking for the justices to reverse the state high court’s decision and hold that federal law preempts Boulder’s claims. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Suncor Energy will not tell the public if Boulder’s effort to hold polluters accountable will succeed. Rather, the decision will tell the public if Boulder’s effort can even proceed in the first place. The path the court will choose is not an entirely foregone conclusion: Although the court routinely takes the side of corporate power over people and the planet, Justice Sam Alito’s last-minute recusal from the case means Boulder only needs one Republican justice to defect to produce a stalemate that leaves the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision in place. Monday’s oral argument provided the first bit of insight into whether any of the GOP justices seem moveable in this case, or if they remain united in support of the fossil fuel industry. Representing the oil companies on Monday was Kannon Shanmugam, head of the Supreme Court litigation practice at Davis Polk. Shanmugam characterized Boulder’s case as “unprecedented,” and argued that the Constitution does not permit individual localities to “use state law to regulate global conduct.” Sarah Harris, principal deputy solicitor general in Trump’s Justice Department, also participated in the oral argument as amicus, and made similar calls for impunity. Harris claimed that Boulder was trying to hold companies liable for “all their fossil fuel activities worldwide.” According to Harris, Boulder’s “entire thesis” depended on the idea that the “mere fact of having injuries” empowered it to regulate “worldwide conduct.” Notably, Colorado’s trial court rejected this line of attack years ago, because it fundamentally misstates what Boulder is trying to do. Boulder County’s lawsuit is not some novel attempt by a municipality to regulate greenhouse emissions around the world, and it does not purport to control any activity outside of its borders. All Boulder is trying to do is get oil companies to help pay for the costs of their allegedly vast deception around the causes of climate change—still needing to be determined in court—and local damage to the environment. As the trial court put it, “the energy companies are arguing against a case the local governments did not plead.” Justice Elena Kagan disposed of this argument with similar ease on Monday, and highlighted that Boulder’s lawsuit “follows the same model” as Big Tobacco lawsuits in the 1990s and, more recently, opioid litigation. There too, Kagan explained, companies made “misrepresentations” that led to “overuse” of their products, producing devastating consequences that state and local governments were able to recover for under state law. “This is the same kind of lawsuit against the same kind of actors for the same kind of harm,” she said. Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, however, failed to appreciate the difference between normal tort liability for in-state injuries and regulation of interstate pollution, which Kavanaugh repeatedly insisted was a “federal law matter.” Kavanaugh, for instance, argued that Boulder’s case can’t be analogized to previous tobacco and opioid cases because, under the court’s precedents, “air and water pollution are different.” Barrett also asked the attorney representing Boulder County, Kevin Russell, to explain why a state may not pass a law “purporting to cap emissions in the other 49 states” but “the same thing can happen through the tort suit.” Russell’s explanation was simple: “It isn’t the same thing,” he said. Crucially, he said, the tort suit wouldn’t prohibit the companies from engaging in any conduct; it only requires the companies to pay for some of the damage that conduct causes. Kavanaugh called this response “a little cavalier,” and warned that “enough of these” lawsuits could “bankrupt” the fossil fuel industry. “So why is the state tort suit different than the state law?” Kavanaugh continued. “I’m just not understanding that.” Kavanaugh’s open worry for the economic prospects of oil and gas companies is connected to a broader fear of too much justice, expressed by both the companies and by some of his Republican colleagues on the bench. Justice Clarence Thomas asked Russell to identify a “limiting principle” for who could be sued under Boulder County’s legal theory. Russell named multiple constitutional limitations, but Shanmugam still claimed on rebuttal that there was “no limit,” and that they risked lawsuits from at least “90,000 municipalities.” Chief Justice John Roberts also asked Russell if, should Boulder County prevail before the court, there would be “at least 50” new lawsuits the “next day,” filed by “a municipality in every single state.” All they would have to do is “copy your pleadings,” Roberts suggested. Russell responded that nothing in the Constitution says preemption arises whenever “a state law, if copied in other states, could cause a lot of litigation.” Basically, the idea that polluters have caused too much harm to have to pay for all of it is more of a personal problem than a legal one. In fairness, Roberts did seem to recognize some problems with the breadth of the immunity that the oil companies were asking for, as did Justice Gorsuch. When Shanmugam argued that Boulder was attempting to restrain out-of-state conduct, Roberts pushed Shanmugam to concede that there are situations where someone who “engages in conduct in State B” that “causes harm to somebody in State A” can be “sued under the law of State A.” When Shanmugam argued that none of the harm Boulder alleged was “directed at Colorado,” Roberts asked why it should make a difference if the person in State B was “aiming at C” but “hit somebody in A.” When Harris suggested that even inaction by Congress could have a preemptive effect on state court proceedings, Gorsuch reacted with mild disbelief. “Nobody can sue at all?” he asked. Roberts’ and Gorsuch’s inquiries touched on the heart of Suncor, and the impunity problem in which the court plays a central part. As the federal government’s response to the climate crisis ranges from disinterest to disdainful, state and local governments have had to ask: Can’t anyone do anything about this harm? Again and again, the court’s answer has been no. Now the prospect of accountability turns on getting a single Republican justice to say yes. Madiba K. Dennie is the Deputy Editor and Senior Contributor at Balls & Strikes. She is the author of The Originalism Trap: How Extremists Stole the Constitution and How We the People Can Take it Back, and her writing has been featured in outlets including The Atlantic and The Washington Post. title: Read the Bold Print: What Palazzo v. Bayview Means for Bankruptcy Disclaimers - JDSupra
content:
Once a debtor files a bankruptcy petition, the stay kicks in and collection activity must grind to a halt to avoid exposing the creditor to liability. While the automatic stay prohibits creditors from attempting to collect on a debt, the stay does not eliminate the need to communicate altogether. Creditors typically still need to send certain account statements or provide other pertinent documents to a debtor about their account. But what should the creditor do when certain notifications may be in direct contravention of the automatic stay of the Bankruptcy Code? The Fourth Circuit’s recent decision in Palazzo v. Bayview Loan Servicing, LLC, provides welcome clarity. The court held that sending certain statements and communications will not violate the automatic stay, provided the appropriate disclaimers are included. Ruben Palazzo filed a Chapter 13 bankruptcy petition in February 2016, to reorganize his debts. During his bankruptcy, his mortgage servicers continued sending him monthly account statements and 1098 tax forms, along with payoff statements that Palazzo had personally requested. Palazzo sued, alleging that those communications were efforts to collect on a debt which are prohibited by the automatic stay and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA). The district court ultimately sided with the mortgage servicer, which was upheld on appeal. The Court scrutinized the specific language in each of the communications. The Monthly Statements and Payoff Statements each provided a breakdown of the outstanding balance, the current interest rate, and other fees and amounts that would become due after the bankruptcy concluded. Critically, each statement included a prominent bankruptcy disclaimer that expressly notified the debtor that the statement was being sent “for informational and compliance purposes only” and that they were “not an attempt to collect a debt against [the debtor].” The Court found that the disclaimers were “clear and unequivocal,” and that a reasonable reader in Palazzo’s position would have understood that no payment was being demanded.  More importantly, Palazzo himself had requested the payoff statements, which undercut his argument that they were sent as an attempt to collect on a debt, rather than a ministerial response to his inquiry. The 1098 tax statements similarly contained information about the interest paid and remaining principal for tax purposes. While those statements did not contain any specific disclaimers, the Court held that they were clearly being sent to provide information to a debtor, necessary for him to complete his taxes. Because of that, the Court found that providing those forms did not evidence an intent to collect. The Palazzo decision confirms what careful creditors have long practiced, and it offers a blueprint for anyone who needs to communicate with a bankrupt debtor. Should a debtor allege a stay violation based on routine correspondence, the Palazzo framework provides a strong defense—so long as your communications contained proper disclaimers and did not demand payment. But be careful not to become complacent and treat all communications similarly. As noted, the Court paid particular attention to the exact wording of the disclaimers provided, and the facts surrounding those communications. As a result, careful drafting of form communications and periodic review of disclaimer language is important to ensure that there is no inadvertent violation of the automatic stay. Consult your attorney before sending notices to debtors who are in a pending bankruptcy proceeding or have received a discharge. title: Grand openings: what four introductions in Suncor v. Boulder show about starting a brief - SCOTUSblog
content: When the court opens its term on Monday with the blockbuster case Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, the justices will have digested four principal briefs. They are Suncor Energy and the other energy companies’ opening brief (Kannon Shanmugam), the United States’ amicus brief supporting the energy companies (Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris), Boulder’s brief (Kevin Russell), and the energy companies’ reply. The merits question is whether federal law bars state-law claims for injuries attributed to interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions. But this post is for anyone who writes briefs, in the Supreme Court or in any court, and it is about the introduction: the prime real estate that offers the court a frame for all the law and facts to follow. Each introduction combines, in its own recipe, the four techniques I outline in my book on legal advocacy, “Point Made”: Brass Tacks, the narrative lens explaining “who, what, when, where, why, how.” The Short List, the logical lens numbering your path to victory. Why Should I Care?, the pragmatic lens giving the court a reason to want to find for you. And Flashpoint, the contrasting lens drawing a line in the sand. The way each side navigates these introductions, each under 1,000 words, also reveals what it sees as its strengths and weaknesses. Even, or especially, when the legal issues are abstract, the best introductions spin a narrative line showing how the parties reached an impasse and how the court should guide them out of it. Call it a Tale of Four Briefs. What story does each tell? For the energy companies: A city and a county in Colorado have sued “two of the world’s countless fossil-fuel producers” for local harms at the end of a global chain, in which production and marketing “resulted in consumers’ use of fossil fuels around the world, which released . . . emissions, which combined with all other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere to alter the global climate, which then resulted in localized physical harms in Boulder.” There’s the causal chain in one sentence. For the government: A single city wants the law of a single state to dictate how the world addresses a global problem: by penalizing conduct “outside Colorado,” much of it “entirely overseas,” for harms in Boulder “from wildfire damage to public-health costs.” The introduction also issues a verdict on this tale: “Absolutely not.” For Boulder: Petitioners “have run to this Court at the case’s outset” to ask for a rule that Congress, not courts, should make. The case is “far from final judgment,” and the Colorado Supreme Court has not yet decided whether respondents have stated a claim under state law. It’s a procedural tale of when and why, but with no concrete narrative of local injuries: Boulder never appears, and Colorado appears only in the name of its highest court. Recounting the injury tale would mean tracing the energy companies’ causal chain; the procedural opening keeps the focus instead on institutional authority and timing. For the energy companies’ reply: Four sentences recast the energy companies’ account of who, what, and why as propositions that, the reply says, Boulder “do[es] not dispute.” That is Brass Tacks used to pull the court back to the energy companies’ story – and to ask the court to treat its factual premises as common ground so that the fight is over their legal effects. The Short List consists of the three or four points you would make to a judge who gave you only 60 seconds to speak. The points must also work as a unit: what does each of these promise, and do they relate to one another as rungs (each a fallback for the one above), gates (reasons the court can abstain from action), or axes (independent grounds that add up)? Here is how I would distill each introduction’s path to victory. (By “introduction” I mean each brief’s opening overview, labeled or not.) The energy companies’ opening brief: rungs on a ladder, all resting on one premise – that the claims target interstate and international emissions Boulder: gates, loosely speaking, united by restraint (who decides, when, and by what method) The energy companies’ reply: the opening list, restructured and reinforced Why Should I Care? Give the court a reason to want to find for you This technique gives the court a reason to feel good about finding for you, usually by triggering one of three judicial fears if it were to decide the other way: misconstruing a doctrine or statute; creating new duties, rules, or defenses; or reaching an unfair result or causing harm. Gauge this part of the introduction by the anxiety it triggers or relieves. The energy companies’ opening brief: an unfair result and harm, at national scale, without naming petitioner ExxonMobil in the introduction, which keeps attention on harm to others rather than on the petitioners themselves The government: harm to the federal system, tested through a hypothetical Boulder: misconstruing a doctrine and creating a new rule, a matter of method rather than scale The reply: the opening brief’s scale argument, compressed into two images Notice, too, that Boulder does not foreground residents’ injuries in the introduction. Rather, Boulder includes those harms at the start of the opening statement instead. The effect is to keep the opening focused on institutional authority and procedural restraint rather than on the causal chain that the energy companies emphasize. A Flashpoint draws a line in the sand between two competing views of the dispute so that you can preempt your opponent’s attempts to make the case into something it’s not. The energy companies’ opening brief: scale, global against local, which makes the suit itself sound unprecedented The energy companies make the state-tort litigation sound novel and the principles barring it settled. Boulder makes the state-law remedies sound ordinary and the proposed bar novel. Both sides want the same advantage: to make the other side explain why the court should depart from familiar ground. Before you file, ask whether your introduction does the same. Ross Guberman is the president of Legal Writing Pro LLC and the founder of BriefCatch LLC. Ahead of the November general election, the Southern California News Group compiled a list of questions to pose to the candidates who wish to represent you. You can find the full questionnaire below. Other political positions held: Palmdale Planning Commissioner Campaign website or social media: vjse5palmdalealive.com How can the city best meet the demand and mandates for more housing, including at lower price points, while also preserving local control and the quality of life for existing neighborhoods and residents? (Please limit your answer to 200 words or less.) The city can best meet the demand and mandates for more housing by ensuring housing developers and investors ascertain the median income of those currently living in the community in which they plan to build, and ensure that the homes or units they build are affordable, reasonable, and match the income of that community. As a city, we should not bar housing development, but we should regulate the way housing is being established in our communities to ensure people do not go into debt or bankruptcy because of mortgages or rents they cannot afford. Banks, realtors, insurance companies, and city government play a role in making sure that this process is fair, reasonable, and affordable for residents. How should the city balance rising costs, paying off debts, such as pension liabilities, and building reserves, all while meeting residents’ needs? Should a solution involve finding new revenue, economic development, trimming the budget, or something else entirely? (Please limit your answer to 200 words or less.) The city can balance rising costs by generating more revenue in our city. We should invest in a universal theme park in our city that will generate year-round revenue — not just revenue in a month or a quarter. We have land and potential investors to make this happen. We need to create more activities in Palmdale to bring jobs back to our city. We lost Staples and Vons on the Eastside of Palmdale. We need to bring them back. We must engage in an audit of our city budget and ascertain where we are spending most of our money and determine whether it is wise or unwise to do so. The investments that the city currently has must be analyzed to see if the city is making a profit from them, such as DryTown Water Park and other similar investments around the city. The city should apply for more grants to help renovate Palmdale Boulevard to make it an attractive city to come to for jobs, wealth, and growth. The city must invest in our local businesses with a Request for Proposals (RFP) when considering what projects need to be done in Palmdale. As a city, we must go local before we go external and global. This can help save the city unnecessary costs by investing in our local businesses where we have amazing talent and giftedness. I also believe the city can address the needs of residents while being fiscally responsible with respect to how it spends its money. We have to look at which projects are working for the city and which ones are not, or have potential to work. At the same time, we must have a reserve fund to ensure that we can meet any crisis that may need our city’s attention. The only way this happens is by good leadership that works and leadership bold enough to make hard, tough, and sometimes controversial decisions. The public expects transparency from public leaders in spending and governance. How can this be achieved? How can the city do better in this area? (Please limit your answer to 200 words or less.) I am a strong proponent of our city being very transparent with the city budget. The city must undergo an audit by a reputable firm, preferably a firm in our city, to ascertain how money is being spent and to whom city contracts constantly go without thorough examination or review. The city should create a webpage on its website specifically dedicated to the city budget, how it’s being spent, what it is about to spend money on, whether it reached out to local businesses first before offering contracts to others, and solicit community input on things the city is contemplating spending money on. The city should provide audit reports quarterly or every six months to residents regarding how city money is being spent. Because the City Council has members in five respective districts, each member should commit to holding town hall meetings in their respective district on how money is being spent by the City Council, and be willing to hear, accept, and receive feedback from the residents on their ideas and suggestions regarding city spending. In your opinion, what is the biggest need your city faces, and how would you address it? (Please limit your answer to 200 words or less.) I think the biggest need our city faces is job growth and economic stability. We still have too many residents traveling to Los Angeles and other cities to make a decent living. Palmdale has so much potential, land, and innovation to make it the number one job growth city in the state of California. We have aviation in our backyard, healthcare, law, construction jobs, and so much more to create more job growth in our city. While we are bringing businesses to our community, we are equally losing businesses in our city as well. Accordingly, we must devise incentives to attract businesses to our city for sustainable longevity and not temporary passivity. With job growth, we can create more housing to address the unhoused in our community. With job growth, we can have more health facilities to address mental health, which has become a major concern in our community. With job growth, we can increase public safety to stop theft and other crimes from happening in our city. With job growth, we can create meaningful jobs for our youth to learn business ownership, entrepreneurship, and trade skills. With job growth, we can create a veterans hospital in the Antelope Valley so our veterans do not have to go down to Wilshire Boulevard to receive assistance. With job growth, our seniors will not have to pay to attend any facilities hosted or sponsored by the city. Our veterans and senior citizens deserve to be treated with the highest dignity and respect for their dedication and service to our community and nation. With job growth, we can create a city on the pathway to prosperity and longevity. Why would you make a good leader, and how would you represent the diverse communities of your city? (Please limit your answer to 200 words or less.) We need more than leadership in Palmdale. We need leadership that works. Leadership that works means having a bold vision for Palmdale’s growth and then going into action to make it a reality. The greatness of Palmdale can be found in the size of the vision and the courage of its actions. We need leadership that doesn’t rest on “we can’t,” but rather “how can we” make our city better than it is. Leadership that works means we can renovate Palmdale Boulevard and have it reflect the majestic presence of our City Hall, the seat of government. Leadership that works means we can finally work to rebuild our Palmdale Airport. Leadership that works means that we can build a Universal Theme park similar to Disneyland and others to generate year-round revenue. Leadership that works means that we provide a state-of-the-art youth center that includes sport and play, entertainment and education. Leadership that works means we make our city budget transparent, and that we provide genuine, authentic, and honest leadership to the people we serve. Leadership that works means that we treat every human being with dignity, respect, and humanity. Leadership that works means we acknowledge our diversity, our culture, and our heritage. Leadership that works means that when a segment of our community is being targeted by overreaching government intrusion, we stand up and speak truth to power and protect the most vulnerable of our society. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) must not become the ruling force in our community, overriding dignity, respect, and humanity. We don’t just need leadership — we need leadership that works. Every resident’s voice must be heard. Dissent breeds democracy, not anarchy. Leadership that works means that, as leaders, we must provide a venue for dissent to be heard and not silenced. I want to hear from all of our Palmdale residents, transcendent of race, color, or creed. title: Ireland v Kazakhstan World Cup playoff: Team news, kick-off time, where to watch - The Irish Times
content:
Carla Ward’s Republic of Ireland side will play Kazakhstan in the first leg of their Women’s World Cup qualifying first-round playoff on Friday. The game at the Astana Arena, in the Kazak capital Astana, will kick-off at the unusual time of 12pm on Friday. The second leg will take place at Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Tuesday at 7.30pm. Ireland are missing a few key players for the game in Astana. Katie McCabe and Marissa Sheva are suspended, while Denise O’Sullivan is nursing a knee injury she picked up with her club, but all three should be available for the second leg in Cork. Meanwhile, Tara O’Hanlon (hamstring) and Saoirse Noonan (ankle) have been ruled out for both fixtures due to injury. Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft is the surprise inclusion, qualifying through her Sligo grandmother. Heather Payne returns to the squad for the first time in a year after spell hampered by injury. Goalkeepers: Courtney Brosnan (Everton), Grace Moloney (Southampton), Sophie Whitehouse (Charlton Athletic). Defenders: Aoife Mannion (Newcastle United), Heather Payne (Leicester City), Anna Patten (Aston Villa), Caitlin Hayes (Brighton), Jessie Stapleton (Leicester City), Megan Connolly (Lazio), Hayley Nolan (Crystal Palace), Chloe Mustaki (Nottingham Forest), Katie McCabe (Chelsea). Midfielders: Denise O’Sullivan (Gotham FC), Marissa Sheva (Sunderland), Aoibheann Clancy (Watford), Jamie Finn (Burnley), Lucy Quinn (Sheffield United), Tyler Toland (Burnley), Jess Ziu (Leicester City), Shanade Hopcroft (Crystal Palace). Forwards: Kyra Carusa (HB Køge), Amber Barrett (Strasbourg), Abbie Larkin (Crystal Palace), Emily Murphy (Brighton), Leanne Kiernan (Newcastle United). Yes. Tickets are still available for the game at Páirc Uí Chaoimh, selling for a very reasonable €30. The winner of these first-round playoffs over the two legs proceeds to the second (and final) round, where a stiffer challenge awaits in the form of Belgium or Poland. Of the eight second-round playoff winners, seven will qualify for the World Cup, while the eighth (based on league phase rankings) has another shot at qualification through the inter-confederation playoffs. Ireland are 21st in the world rankings and currently play in Nations League A, while Kazakhstan are ranked 98th and compete in the third-tier League C. Looking further down the line, Ireland beat Poland twice (at home and away) earlier this year, and in last year’s Nations League beat Belgium 4-2 in the first-leg relegation/promotion playoff in Dublin before losing 2-1 in the return leg four days later. So, in short, they’re both opponents Ireland are capable of beating. But first, they must do the job in Kazakhstan on Friday if they’re to stay on track for a place at next year’s World Cup in Brazil. title: "Coyote v. Acme" dodged the Acme anvil, landed a hit of its own - Daily Bruin
content: Wile E. Coyote stares into the camera at night. “Coyote vs. Acme,” the most recent live-action/animation hybrid “Looney Tunes” film, was released Aug. 28 by distributor Ketchup Entertainment. (Courtesy of IMDb) Beep beep! No need to chase down the latest internet and box office sensation: “Coyote vs. Acme” is a sure catch. The most recent live-action/animation hybrid “Looney Tunes” film has seen nothing but success for distributor Ketchup Entertainment. Released in theaters Aug. 28, “Coyote vs. Acme” earned $15.5 million domestically in its opening weekend, debuting in second place at the North American box office after “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and grossing over $100 million globally before its streaming release. While those numbers would be impressive on their own, the film’s against-all-odds triumph is all the sweeter given that Warner Bros. Discovery shelved the film in 2023 for a $30 million tax write-off. Beyond its box office success, “Coyote vs. Acme” has become a social media sensation, reaching well beyond its intended family audience with fan art, fan fiction, cosplay and countless edits of Wile E. Coyote and the Road Runner set to Chappell Roan’s “Casual.” But why, of all movies, has a courtroom family comedy built around a nearly century-old intellectual property become so popular? “Coyote vs. Acme” balances updating a familiar franchise without abandoning what made it so beloved – exactly what people need right now. There is an underdog story both on and off the screen. The outcry that brought the film back only strengthened its message of the little guy. In this case, Wile E. Coyote and his lawyer Kevin Avery (Will Forte) take on the Acme Corporation, a corrupt manufacturing conglomerate. In a time when companies seem to care less and less about consumers and monopolies feel all but inevitable, the reassurance that individuals can and do make a difference is vital for audiences of all ages. [Related: Film Review: In gripping, clever ‘Primetime,’ the pursuit of justice becomes unjust] This relevance, however, is just scratching the surface. One smaller, almost throwaway moment in the film actually reflects one of its deeper strengths. While showcasing Acme products, Granny uses predator spray on Pepé Le Pew – a meta-joke acknowledging the skunk’s longstanding portrayal of unwanted “romantic” pursuit as comedy. As some older properties – notably Disney – attempt to erase problematic elements from their past, the “Looney Tunes” franchise’s willingness to acknowledge and poke fun at its own history is refreshing and commendable. One particularly interesting response to the film has been the aforementioned fan shipping of Wile E. Coyote and the Road Runner, seemingly fueled by the widely reposted courtroom scene in which the Road Runner asks if Coyote is coming back. Whether the moment was intentionally romantic is almost irrelevant, as fans’ interpretation of the duo has brought the characters into the modern age. While the film makes some refreshing updates, “Coyote vs. Acme” remains true to its source material. That may not sound particularly groundbreaking when so many fans feel betrayed by their favorite franchises being altered by corporate influence for financial gain, but it is a much greater feat than it was even 10 years ago. The movie is not a direct sequel like its major box office competition. Instead, it’s a loving tribute and continuation of the previously time-constrained Wile E. Coyote-Road Runner shorts, which certainly added to the outpouring of support for the movie. Though based on a New Yorker column by Ian Frazier, the semi-original story is just another tally for “Coyote vs. Acme” that makes it a hit with audiences who have been begging for more originality for years. The film uses traditional animation in an age dominated by artificially created or assisted art. More striking is the creativity behind the fan content, including original art and romantic interpretations of the central cartoon characters. Many celebrate “Coyote vs. Acme” as one of the first true family movies in some time, appealing to adults through its courtroom comedy and children through its cartoonish humor. In recent releases, a lot of content aimed at children has been made with children and marketable merchandise in mind. This movie, by contrast, is seemingly more focused on its story and characters – another celebrated departure from its competition. All these elements set the movie apart, but one central highlight remains: “Coyote vs. Acme” balances its changes while playing on nostalgia. The film has all the updating and differentiating necessary to make it refreshing while still instilling a sentimental feeling in its adult audience. That compromise is what truly makes the movie what audiences need to see – comfort in change. They “fought the law and the law won,” but “Coyote vs. Acme” won something Warner Bros. Discovery couldn’t put a price on: the love and respect of its many fans. small studio guest house for rent (one room, fully furnished) with kitchenette, small bathroom and a/c. great location, close to ucla. century city and freeways. plenty of street parking. available for rent after oct 5. $1650 per month great, quiet , safe residential neighborhood. if interested call karen 310 508 1963 or email kphankinson@yahoo.com

title: There's A Honda SUV For Every Type Of Buyer Right Now - CarBuzz
content:
Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update In the last decade or so, the SUV has gradually become the most popular vehicle segment within the automotive industry. The combination of utility, space and comfy ride quality are the primary reasons why customers favor them over the traditional sedan. If you are looking for a reliable and efficient SUV model in 2026, there is a high chance that you might come across a Honda model. This iconic Japanese brand has a wide range of SUV models available, and we are here to guide you through all the best Honda SUV models you can buy right now in 2026. This article examines all the Honda SUV models on sale in 2026. All pricing and data are correct at the time of writing; the automaker may change or update these at any time. MSRP, where quoted, excludes destination fees and other costs. The HR-V has always been on the affordable end of the spectrum when it comes to Honda's SUV products. Since this small crossover was introduced back in 2016, it has been loved by customers for its excellent space utilization and unique styling. While the original HR-V was based on the same platform as the smaller Honda Jazz/Fit. The current HR-V is in its third-generation, which was introduced to the US market in 2023. Unlike the previous generation, the third-gen HR-V is now based on the same platform as the popular Honda Civic, which gives the HR-V a bigger exterior stance and a sleek and sporty design. The interior is also more spacious on the third-gen HR-V as well, with 37.7 inches of rear legroom and a total of 55.1 cubic feet of space in its max configuration. The powertrain leans more towards efficiency, as the HR-V is powered by a naturally aspirated inline-four engine that produces 158 horsepower and 138 pound feet of torque. Front-wheel drive comes as standard, but you can also opt for all-wheel drive if you require some extra traction on rough terrain. As for the fuel efficiency, the FWD model gets the best mileage with a combined 28 MPG, the AWD model follows behind with a fuel mileage of 27 combined MPG. Being the entry-level SUV within the Honda lineup, the HR-V also has a starting price that's friendly for buyers who are tight on their budget. There are three trim levels available for the 2027 model year. There's the base LX trim to start with. In the middle, you have the Sport and the EX-L at the very top. The LX and Sport both have a sub-30K price tag, while the EX-L exceeds slightly over the 30K bar. While many may reckon a sub-30k starting price means a vehicle with poor value and little features, the HR-V proves otherwise. The entry-level EX comes with an entire suite of Honda Sensing Safety features. On top of that, you also get wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Upgrading to the Sport trim gets you a bigger 18-inch wheel, smart entry, remote engine start as well as heated front seats with a price tag well below $30K. The HR-V may not have the biggest interior space and the most powerful engine, but in terms of price and value, it's the perfect option if you don't want to break the bank. The Honda CR-V is very likely the first model that comes to mind when talking about Honda SUV models. This compact crossover has been Honda's bestseller for years and remains one of the most recognizable and best Honda SUVs till this day. And when it comes to the question of "What is the best Honda SUV to buy?", the Honda CR-V will always be the best answer to that question. The CR-V was first introduced to the US market in 1997. With a rugged exterior look and impressive interior quality, the CR-V soon became popular among US buyers, setting the tone for its later success. The current sixth-gen CR-V was introduced in 2023. It adopts an appearance that's similar to the latest Honda models at the time, while the boxy exterior silhouette still gives this Honda SUV a spacious interior, one of the best in its class. Unlike most of the Honda SUV models currently on sale, the CR-V offers multiple powertrain options for customers to choose from. There is a traditional gasoline inline-four engine that produces 190 horsepower. For those seeking a more efficient option, the sixth-gen CR-V gets Honda's latest hybrid system, which develops 204 horsepower and a whooping 40 mpg combined with the most efficient FWD model. If neither the gasoline nor the hybrid powertrain sounds interesting to you, there is another third option that's truly unique and groundbreaking. The CR-V e:FCEV is America's first production plug-in hydrogen fuel cell EV. This unique version of CR-V offers multiple power sources and is only available for purchase at select dealerships in California. What makes the CR-V e:FCEV special is the fact that it combines plug-in capability with FCEV technology together in one vehicle. A fuel cell vehicle like the CR-V e:FCEV generates electricity using a process that combines hydrogen and oxygen together. The plug-in capability also allows the e:FCEV to drive full on electric and charge up at a charging station like a traditional battery electric vehicle. The CR-V e:FCEV gets 174 horsepower from an electric motor driving the front wheels; it also comes with an EPA-rated range of 270 miles, and a hefty price tag of $50,000. 2024 Honda Prologue front 3/4 angle in blue while charging 2024 Honda Prologue front 3/4 angle in blue while charging While Honda was known for making high-revving gasoline and efficient hybrid vehicles throughout the years, the electric vehicle has never been an area that the company was deeply invested in. The Honda Prologue marks the only Honda electric model you can buy now in 2026. This electric crossover sits between the CR-V and the off-road-focused Passport. It's no news that the Prologue is essentially a rebadged Chevrolet Blazer EV, but Honda has tried its best to make sure the Prologue looks and feels like a Honda from first glance. To start with, the exterior of the Prologue was done by the Honda Design Studio located in Los Angles. The reworked exterior gives the prologue a clean and modern look that distinguishes itself from the American sibling. There are two powertrains available for the Prologue in 2026. There is a single motor front-wheel drive model which delivers more range and efficiency. If you would like a more punchy powertrain, a 300 horsepower dual motor is also there at your disposal. The days of Honda Prologue are in the final count down as of 2026, as Honda had announced earlier this year that the sales of Prologue will conclude after the 2026 model year. The discontinuation of Prologue can be contributed to several reasons, the main contributor being the discontinuation of federal tax credits for battery electric vehicles since last year. Combine the above reasons with a rising tariff being applied to vehicles manufactured outside the US (Prologue was made in Mexico), it's not a surprise that Honda finally pulled the plug on their only EV. Thus making 2026 the last and only chance to get your hands on this Honda electric SUV. For those with a bigger family and require an extra row of seats, the Honda Pilot is the only SUV within Honda's current lineup that will satisfy your needs. Ever since the Pilot was introduced in 2003, this three-row Honda SUV already has a huge focus on interior space and usability. As of 2026, the Honda Pilot is in its fourth generation and has just received a facelift in the 2025 model year. The facelift brought several exterior upgrades such as a redesigned front fascia and new wheels while the interior also received a couple of new features such as 5G connectivity and a power tailgate. The powertrain on the Honda Pilot is the old-school naturally aspirated V6 that we are familiar with. Even without the assistance of a turbo or an electric motor, this V6 is still capable of 285 horsepower and 262 pound feet of torque. The engine is paired with a 10-speed automatic transmission while the front-wheel drive comes as standard with optional all-wheel drive for those who need the extra traction. "It may not be the quickest or most efficient vehicle in its class, but the J Series V6 on the Pilot sounds fantastic as it hits peak power at 6,100 rpm and peak torque at 5,000 rpm. If you enjoy the noise from a classically-sweet engine, the Pilot doesn't disappoint." If you were to put all the Honda SUVs currently on sale into a direct comparison, the Pilot is certainly the winner when it comes to interior space and cargo capacity. Apart from the fact that it has an extra row and seating for seven people, the Pilot also has loads of space inside the cabin. To start with, the Pilot is able to offer 40.2 inches of headroom for the second row passenger and 39.3 inches for the third row passenger. When it comes to headroom, it has 40.8 inches for the second row and 32.5 inches for the people seated in the third row. On top of that, the Pilot also has 87 cubic feet of cargo space in its maximum configuration, making it one of the most spacious options when compared to other rivals within the same segment. 2026 Honda Pilot Interior Dimensions & Cargo Capacity The new Honda Passport has an appearance that shouts its outdoor spirit at first glance. The rugged exterior design along with some off-road-ready details, the new fourth-gen Passport is no longer a dull urban SUV, but rather it is a Honda SUV with the ability to tackle rough terrain. The Passport was first introduced back in the 1990s, in which the first ever Honda Passport was actually a rebadged Isuzu Rodeo. Throughout the years, the Passport has gradually become an SUV with some serious off-road capability. The fourth-gen Passport was introduced in 2026 with a brand-new design. Ditching the family-focused design of the previous generation, Honda has given the new Passport a rugged and aggressive exterior design. On top of that, this fourth-gen Passport also has some huge focus on its off-road capabilities. Underneath the hood you will find the same 3.5-liter V6 powertrain that powers the Honda Pilot. All-wheel drive comes as standard to emphasize its off-road ability, while a 10-speed automatic transmission delivers a smooth and seamless gear shift. Other than the rugged exterior look and a smooth V6 powertrain, the Passport is also one of the most reliable Honda SUVs you can buy right now. The Passport scores 82 out of 100 in the reliability ranking by JD Power. As for the recalls and complaints, the new fourth-gen Passport only received a single recall and 63 complaints according to NHTSA, once again illustrating the dependability of Honda models. To maximize the off-road capability of your Honda Passport, the Trailsport is definitely the one you want to get if you are planning to take this Honda SUV deep into the wild. Compared to the base RTL trims, the Trailsport receive a handful of features and upgrades to help the Passport feel at home when conquering the roughest terrain. To start with, the Trailsport models receive all-terrain tires and off-road tuned suspension as standard. On top of that, you also get skid plats underneath the floor to protect the drivetrain during off-road conditions. Another feature that is only found on the Trailsport model is the TrailWatch camera system. This system provides dynamic tire path graphics to show the driver where the vehicle will travel, which makes it easier to navigate through rough conditions. As for the appearance, you get amber hood lights and amber daytime running lights along with a high visibility recovery hook and cloth seats with Trailsport stitching and accents to remind people of the off-road spirit of Trailsport models. title: They Told Me I Have Factor V Leiden 15 Years Ago, But Was Told Not to Worry: Karen's Story - National Blood Clot Alliance
content:
Two weeks later she had a clot in her leg and a PE. I was the only one and found out I have it heterozygous. My doctor at the time said I shouldn’t worry — I was probably just a carrier. I woke up at 10:15 pm with pain in my right shoulder blade. After 45 minutes of excruciating pain, it didn’t go away. By the way, two years ago I was diagnosed with lymphoma — so I have a hematologist. No treatments, just watching. The ER did a CT and found multiple bilateral PE and infarction. They put me on heparin and transferred me to another hospital. I met with a pulmonologist. They ordered an echocardiogram — it was normal. Then a deep vein leg ultrasound, venous duplex — and bingo. They think the lymphoma coupled with Factor V Leiden is my culprit. I have been back to ER with pain but was told it was transfer pain and that the clots are dissolving. I love reading the stories and seeing that I am not alone. A brother just had surgery yesterday and they tested him — no results yet. Phone: 703.935.8845

title: Pennsylvania gubernatorial election: Garrity v. Krawchuk v. Shapiro - wesanews.org
content: What’s at stake: The race for governor is the only statewide contest on the 2026 ballot, and it is commanding attention for another reason: Incumbent Gov. Josh Shapiro is often considered a potential 2028 presidential candidate. And whether he runs or not, the state plays a key role in deciding national elections. In his first term, the Democrat has billed himself as a pragmatist with a “get [expletive] done” agenda, and as a champion of the state willing to oppose President Donald Trump. Along with Lt. Gov. Austin Davis, Shapiro has sought to make the state more economically competitive — though he has said more progress could be made were it not for Republicans who control the state Senate. Shapiro’s Republican rival, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, has sought to use Shapiro’s national profile against him, frequently accusing him of being more focused on Pennsylvania Avenue, where the White House is located, than on Pennsylvania itself. Garrity argues that she and running mate Jason Richey will run the state more efficiently and engineer an economic turnaround. But she has been dramatically outspent by Shapiro, a prodigious fundraiser, and Democrats have criticized her for ties to Trump. The governor is the chief executive for Pennsylvania, a state with 13 million people, tens of thousands of employees and an annual budget of $50 billion. The governor is charged with executing the laws of the state, and overseeing state departments that carry out regulations on everything from health and education policy to economic development and corrections. (Among the responsibilities overseen by the governor's cabinet is setting statewide election policy — a potentially vital position for the 2028 presidential campaign.) The governor signs or vetoes legislation passed by the legislature and is responsible for proposing a budget each year, playing a key role in negotiating the city’s fiscal policy with leaders in the General Assembly. The governor also commands the state National Guard and the state police. The governor’s running mate, meanwhile, assumes the duties of leading the state should the governor die, resign, or be removed or otherwise incapacitated. The lieutenant governor also presides over the state Senate and can cast a tiebreaking vote. Duties also include serving on the state’s Emergency Management Council and chairing the state’s Board of Pardons, which makes recommendations to the governor about pardon applications. Governors serve four-year terms and are limited to serving two consecutive terms. Their salary is adjusted for inflation each year; the position pays $253,870 this year. Lieutenant governors also are limited to two back-to-back terms. The position pays $213,248 in 2026. Stacy Garrity brings to the race a record as an Iraq War veteran — she was widely praised for her oversight of a prison there — and as a business executive. And she can boast of getting almost as many votes as Donald Trump did in 2024, when she won a second term serving as the state’s fiscal manager. In that role, she’s touted her stewardship of the state’s college savings program and other funds in her care. Garrity has long been a staunch conservative and a vocal supporter of Trump, and Republican party leaders helped clear the primary field for Garrity, who would be the state’s first female governor. With her running mate, Allegheny County attorney and former local GOP party chair Jason Richey, she has pledged to “unleash a new era of economic prosperity, make life more affordable for families, renew the American Dream, [and] rebuild trust in our institutions.” Party: RepublicanPlace of residence: Sayre, Bradford CountyEducation: B.A., Bloomsburg University of Pennsylvania; certificate, Cornell University Business Management InstituteCurrent occupation: Pennsylvania Treasurer Related experience: Colonel, U.S. Army Reserve (retired); vice president, Global Tungsten & Powders (retired); trustee, Guthrie Robert Packer Hospital; board of directors, Bradford County United Way Supporters/endorsements: President Donald Trump; Pennsylvania’s Republican Congressional delegation; Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday; Pennsylvania Auditor General Tim DeFoor; more than a dozen Republican state lawmakers; Associated Builders and Contractors, Keystone Chapter and Eastern PA Chapter Total Fundraising* (reported as of Sept. 14): Total raised (2023-2026): $7,359,896.85 Total spent (2023-2026): $6,288,845.31 Many voters are worried about the affordability of everything from gas to groceries and the price of housing. What will you do as governor to address those concerns? Pennsylvania families have been struggling under inflation that is 25% higher than the national rate, while also facing the fifth-highest tax burden in the country. It doesn’t have to be like this. My plan is clear: We will cap property taxes so seniors can stay in the homes they’ve built, and younger Pennsylvanians can build their futures here. We will take on the [Pharmacy Benefit Manager] monopoly and lower prescription drug costs. And we will unleash Pennsylvania’s natural gas so that we can lower the utility costs impacting Pennsylvania families each day. Debate about data center development has been a key issue in this race, but there are also concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence and electronic surveillance systems like Flock. What can you do to keep Pennsylvania competitive in tech industries while addressing public concerns about privacy and job security? The balance between innovation and privacy is a constant struggle, but Pennsylvania has been continually behind the 8-ball. We need a governor who will work to stay ahead of the curve, which is why I have listened to community concerns and called for common sense guardrails on data center development and for the banning of Flock cameras in our communities. Pennsylvania saw a surge in measles cases, and there have long been signs of rising public skepticism when it comes to the efforts of public health agencies to address disease outbreaks. What would you do as governor to restore that trust and ensure Pennsylvania has an effective disease-prevention strategy? Having served three deployments to the Middle East in the U.S. Army Reserve, I have received as many vaccinations as anyone can imagine, and I would encourage the people of Pennsylvania to receive their recommended vaccinations. However, [starting with] the COVID pandemic, people are losing faith in their government’s ability to address public health challenges. COVID-19 lockdowns pale in comparison to the [state Department of Health’s] new 502-page health code revision. [Editor’s note: The revision to which Garrity refers, which set out new regulations for responding to communicable diseases and which Republicans criticized intensely, was withdrawn after the campaigns submitted their responses to the questionnaire. State officials say a new version will be proposed in the future.] We need a governor who will level with the people of Pennsylvania and provide full transparency to the process. The federal government has cut its support for safety-net programs that include food stamps and Medicaid, and a work-requirement for Medicaid recipients will take effect next year. How do you feel about those changes, and what should the state be doing in response to them? Medicaid was established to provide care to pregnant women, mothers with children, people with disabilities, and other vulnerable Americans. Congress took steps to ensure the program supports those it was intended to help. Provisions include work requirements for certain able-bodied adults, stronger enrollment standards, and restrictions on states' ability to use taxes on healthcare providers to finance their share of Medicaid. Pennsylvania's Medicaid program changed assessments on hospitals and managed-care organizations, increasing Medicaid financing by approximately $788 million annually. Healthcare providers are already under significant pressure, particularly in rural communities. The Garrity-Richey Administration will preserve Medicaid for Pennsylvanians who depend on it while working to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse. It’s been a dozen years since either party has had full control of the legislature and governor’s mansion. If you win and your party captures both houses of the legislature, what will be your top legislative priorities? And if the other party maintains its hold on at least one chamber, what key priorities do you think you would share with leaders from across the aisle? My first and foremost priority will be getting Pennsylvania’s economy back on track. Pennsylvania’s economy ranks 47th in the nation and taxpayers face the 5th-highest tax burden in the nation. To put that in perspective, a Pennsylvania family earning $70,000 a year pays between $2,000 and $5,000 more each year in taxes than a comparable family in Florida. That changes in my administration. We’ll work to reduce that tax burden, cut red tape and the regulatory burden that is holding business back, and unleash Pennsylvania’s natural gas reserves — which will produce more than 200,000 good-paying, family-sustaining jobs across our Commonwealth. Krawchuk is a computer programmer and entrepreneur who lives in the Philadelphia suburbs, and — as one would expect from a libertarian candidate — he says the answer to many of Pennsylvania’s woes is to shrink the role of government, with steps that include privatizing public schools and reducing property taxes. This is his third run for governor, after previously vying for the post in 1998 and 2002. His campaign notes he’s “the proud owner of a Tesla Cybertruck and Tesla Model Y, and a long-term Tesla shareholder since 2014.” Krawchuk’s running mate, John Thomas, is a resident of Kittanning, Armstrong County, who previously ran for U.S. Senate against Dave McCormick and Bob Casey. Party: LibertarianPlace of residence: Abington Township, Montgomery CountyEducation: B.S., physics, St. Joseph’s University; graduate, Abington Citizens Police AcademyCurrent occupation: Entrepreneur Related experience: Former candidate for Pennsylvania Governor (1998, 2002, 2018); president of an IT consulting firm; “Student of the Pennsylvania Constitution,” talk radio host and professional public speaker; parliamentarian Many voters are worried about the affordability of everything from gas to groceries and the price of housing. What will you do as governor to address those concerns? Prices are too high because taxes are too high. The cost of Pennsylvania government has been rising at three times the rate of inflation for over 50 years. As governor, I will veto every tax increase and use the line-item veto to eliminate unconstitutional and special interest spending. My website lists over three billion dollars in savings from vetoing dozens of big ticket items, plus little savings like no longer putting the governor’s name on “Welcome to Pennsylvania” signs. Each veto will have a subsequent positive impact on prices. But the biggest money-saving item for individuals is the elimination of the school property tax. title: Milan’s Omari Hutchinson reveals laughing about goal v Manchester United with Ruben Amorim - Yahoo Sports
content: Serie A side Milan signed Omari Hutchinson from Nottingham Forest in the summer transfer window. While the player is yet to show true glimpses of his quality, he has now revealed laughing about his goal against Manchester United with Rossoneri boss Ruben Amorim. The attacker has previously revealed that the impression he made on the Amorim during his spell at Old Trafford helped him earn a move to the San Siro. Hutchinson's first goal in the Premier League, in fact, came against Manchester United and it was also Amorim's first game with the Red Devils. In an interview with SportMediaset, he revealed that he has joked about it with the Milan manager. He said – via MilanNews: "I scored my first goal for Ipswich against him, and it was a great feeling. We joked about it before I came here." He also pointed out the difference between how the game is played in England and how it is played in Italy. "It's been fantastic from the start. I'm enjoying myself here. I'm working really hard. Compared to the Premier League, it's still early to judge, but everything here is very tactical." Hutchinson was also asked about his nickname – the Wizard. He responded: "I chose it because I don't see myself as just Omari Hutchinson but I want to be the best version of myself." Hutchinson is clearly taking his time to adjust to a new life and a new country. He needs that, especially Amorim's system isn't easy to adapt to instantly. This will put him in good stead in the next few weeks, especially as Alexis Saelemaekers is out for the unforeseeable future.

title: Alaska Policy Forum v. Alaska Public Offices Commission - Cato Institute
content: Because Alaska’s decision to treat public policy analysis as campaign speech triggers duties of registration, reporting, and donor disclosure, it is incompatible with the guarantees of the First Amendment. Learn more about Cato’s Amicus Briefs Program. Cato’s latest amicus brief serves to defend the First Amendment interests of an Alaska think tank that regularly opines on matters of public policy. The ability to participate in the marketplace of ideas and express views on such matters should not require mastery of arcane and indeterminate campaign finance law. But when disclosure obligations attach to the exercise of First Amendment rights, an institutional speaker must often determine, even before it speaks, whether publishing will require registration, financial reporting, and the disclosure of the identities of its supporters. The question the case at hand raises is whether the First Amendment allows a state to impose those obligations on an organization that simply publishes discussions of public policy. Alaska Policy Forum, a nonprofit research organization, published materials criticizing ranked-choice voting just before Alaskans considered a ballot initiative to adopt it. APF’s publications never mentioned the initiative by name. The Alaska Public Offices Commission treated them as regulated electoral communications anyway, relying on their language and timing, and found that compensated employee time was the expenditure triggering Alaska’s registration, reporting, and disclosure requirements. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed, and Cato has now filed an amicus brief supporting APF’s petition for certiorari. For more than 50 years, our nation’s Supreme Court has continued to narrow the means by which government may regulate political spending. Compelled disclosure itself burdens association, as NAACP v. Alabama (1958) held. And as McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995) put it, the simple interest in providing voters with additional relevant information does not justify a requirement that a writer make statements or disclosures she would otherwise omit. Alaska’s regime cannot be reconciled with the Court’s jurisprudence. In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), a disclosure provision reached anyone who made expenditures for the purpose of influencing a federal election. The Court held that the ambiguity of that phrase posed constitutional problems, because that phrase could encompass both issue discussion and advocacy of a political result, and construed it to reach only communications expressly advocating the election or defeat of a clearly identified candidate. McConnell v. FEC (2003) later allowed a broader category, but only because BCRA’s definition supplied criteria that were both easily understood and objectively determinable. Alaska’s standard meets neither requirement. The State uses the label of express advocacy but defines that term by what an audience would take a communication to mean, a perspective the speaker cannot know in advance. It asks whether speech, read as a whole and with limited reference to outside events, is susceptible of no other reasonable interpretation than an exhortation to vote, and lets timing and the audience’s presumed knowledge of the ballot decide the result. The Court has twice rejected that method. Buckley declined to analyze the question in terms of intent and of effect, because that perspective would afford no security for free discussion. And in FEC v. Wisconsin Right to Life (2007), the Court rejected tests resting on the actual effect speech will have on an election or on a segment of the target audience, holding that where doubt remains, the tie goes to the speaker, not the censor. Alaska has combined three speech-chilling features: a contextual rule for classifying speech, an expenditure definition that includes ordinary employee time, and a threshold beginning at the first dollar. Together they require a policy organization to conduct its own campaign finance analysis before publishing its own research. Vagueness, as Buckley noted, is particularly treacherous where violation carries criminal penalties. Speakers facing an uncertain boundary steer far wider of the unlawful zone. Speech is chilled even if no penalty ever issues, because the risk of a chilling effect on association is enough. Cato’s brief argues that the Court should grant the petition and reaffirm that the presence of a public question on a ballot does not diminish the freedom to discuss any issue related to it. Director, Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, Cato Institute Every weekday morning: independent analysis grounded in individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and peace.
